scope: One additional reef fish for the guide, illustrative encounters and optional identification. Show an unsexed white/red example with its supporting fin rays braced on a small illustrative branch perch.
iucnYearConvention: LC assessed 3 March 2015; published 2016 with errata in 2017. FishBase current IUCN export supplies the assessment date and status; Museums Victoria corroborates LC and reproduces the publication/errata citation. Direct primary IUCN species-page and DOI access failed. Do not present the errata or publication date as a new assessment.

specimens.name: Longnose hawkfish
marks: A very long pointed snout extends from a slender body
Red lengthwise lines cross red bars to form a grid on a pale body
Tiny tassels rise near the tips of the back-fin spines
Thick lower side-fin rays form sturdy little supports
specimens.role: A reef-perching predator that eats tiny crustaceans from the water and the bottom.
specimens.fact: The small tassels on its back-fin spines are called cirri. Its strong lower side-fin rays help it perch among coral branches.
specimens.habitat: Tropical Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific reefs, especially steep outer slopes with sea fans or black corals. Often found deeper than 25 m.
specimens.behavior: Often rests among branches of gorgonian sea fans and black corals. This specimen shows a perched pose with gentle fin movement; its support is an illustrative branch.
specimens.observe: Follow the red grid, then look for the long snout and tiny dorsal tassels. Compare its slender body with the deeper yellow body of the yellow longnose butterflyfish: a long snout alone is not enough to identify either fish.

claimSupport.acceptedName: The current Eschmeyer catalog, updated 21 September 2026, accepts Oxycirrhites typus Bleeker 1857. Museums and Smithsonian use this name; Oxycirrhites morrisi and O. seftoni are catalogued synonyms.
claimSupport.shape: Australian Museum directly describes the long snout, pale/red grid and dorsal-spine cirri. Smithsonian documents an elongated body, 10 dorsal spines plus 13 soft rays, 2–4 cirri near each spine tip, thick lower 5–6 pectoral rays and a blunt, straight caudal edge. The learning marks simplify these diagnostic characters without promising a complete taxonomic key.
claimSupport.habitatDiet: Museums Victoria describes current-exposed outer slopes and gorgonian/black-coral perches, with small planktonic and benthic crustaceans as food. Australian Museum and Smithsonian independently describe the perches; Smithsonian specifies the lower pectoral rays as supports.
claimSupport.depth: Select the museum Indo-Pacific interval 10–100 m with its usual-below-25 m qualification. Australian Museum says usually below 30 m; Smithsonian reports 5–100 m including shallow eastern Pacific observations. These regional/general differences are retained here rather than treating the chosen interval as an absolute limit or equally suitable at every depth.
claimSupport.size: Museum maximum is 13 cm total length. The model uses an illustrative .12 m fish, including snout and tail; branch support is excluded from that nominal fish-length label. This is not a measured individual or a claim about typical adult size.
claimSupport.conservation: FishBase current IUCN 2025-2 export gives LC and 3 March 2015. Museums Victoria reproduces Greenfield and Williams (2016), errata2017, and independently lists LC. Direct primary IUCN access failed, so no unaccessed rationale or population trend is asserted. Smithsonian’s stale Not evaluated / Listed field is not used.
claimSupport.comparison: The one-way yellow_longnose_butterflyfish link compares two long-snouted forms already supported by the guide; it is an educational contrast, not a nearest-relative or closest-lookalike claim. The older butterflyfish record remains exact.

specimens.caution: No sex, maturity or pair-bond diagnosis from this solitary unsexed model. No aquarium-care, enhanced vision, fluorescence or fixed lifelong perch claim. No assumption that it is restricted to black coral, that all branches are living coral, or that every dive site represents its complete geographic/depth range.
